words: I mean, the way I do mine, I, I have me a pan of cold water and I put tablespoons of salt in that water and stir it up. And then if I core and slice my apples I drop them down in that and they stay white. They don't turn, they don't turn dark. And then, I'll only do enough for maybe 2 or 3 jars.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And then I put it on, cook it.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Yeah, that's all I'm doing.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And the salt that's in the water is just enough, you can't taste the salt. It's just enough to give the fruit a good flavor.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I had lemon juice in that middle batch. You know, water and lemon juice to try to keep it from turning brown. That was okay, but the apples were too tart, and the lemon juice finally got. It wasn't sour, but it wasn't.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Excuse me. The salt will take some of that tartness away too.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Okay. Thank you. Now, I do have some questions to ask you. And these I'm not going to write down, we're just going to converse.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I may not hit all these or we may I may do one here, and we may end up talking about one on the back. Take your time. But these are just some questions that, we've found help people think of things that they might want to say, better than the questions we were asking for. We talked a little bit last night about this, but what do you think are some of the advantages and disadvantages of living in a rural place?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I think it's better for children. They always have something to do. Where in town after they leave school, there's nothing else for them to do. On the farm, the way it was with my kids anyway, they came home from school, they had chores to do, and they didn't think, have time to think about going out and getting into mischief.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And, then I think it we weren't, we weren't one of the, what would you call it?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: We were very small farmers. We didn't have much money. And, our kids had to learn to take care of what things they did have. And I think that's good for kids. Now that they're married, they all know. They know the value of money and how to take care of it. And and how to spend it wisely. Where if it's just handed to them, I, I, I don't think they, appreciate it this much.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And then the air is clear and fresh and I think people just feel better. Of course, we get sick up here too. But then, our air is clear, fresh. Our water is pure.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: It's just a good, clean living, I think. Just good for people to live that way.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: How many disadvantages you see?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Oh, I think every place has its disadvantages. When you get up our age and, and you live out like this, and the winters are long, we get lots of snow. We worry about getting sick and getting out to the doctor. My husband and I both are seriously ill and I think that's a disadvantage. But, my husband was born here and lived out here all his life.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: he doesn't seem to want to live somewhere else, so we just go through it.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: But it, it does worry you.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: It does.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Cause you're so far from a good doctor hospital.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: It does worry you, and that scar.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Is it hard to get groceries?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: No. We both drive and we go, at least twice a month to town for groceries.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I wouldn't say to town, do you mean Orofino?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Mostly Lewiston because that's where our doctors are. And I have to get my blood tested every month. And, so while we're down there, we just get our groceries. Once in a while, we go to Orofino.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: But town, when you say town you mean.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: It means Lewiston, mostly.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Did there use to be a store or anything like that in Teakean or around here?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yes, Mr. (unintelligible), father in law had a store right up here in Teakean.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: And now that's gone.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: That's gone.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: When we were in Kendrick, we were asking some women what worried them about their community. And the thing that worried the most or one of the things was losing the stores and having to go to Lewiston and having to go to to Moscow or someplace to go to get groceries and bread and just the things you basically need every day.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, these big, chain stores are running all the little stores out of business. Again, it's the big taking over the small. Same as it is here on the farm. The big farmers are taking over the small farmers, and pretty soon it's just going to be big farmers. And I suppose it's the same way with their stores. It's going to be the supermarket or nothing.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: How would you compare your life as a woman who's lived on a farm? Almost, well, all your married life, right? Yeah. You married your husband, you moved to his farm and you go through life. How do you compare your life with, say, the life of a woman who who lives in the city?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, I don't know. There's never a dull moment. I know that there's always lots to do. Like I said last night, I've worked side by side with my husband, to do the farming and,

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I did just almost everything on the farm that is to be done. I've milked cows. I've drove tractor. I drove truck.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: You've learned to do things many girls more fortunately situated don't even know needs to be done.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: That's right. And, I had to sew for my children, and back when my children were small, we didn't have mixes and things. Everything was made from scratch. And with four children at home, I baked something almost every day. And then I bake bread once or twice a week. We butchered our own meat. I had to take care of that.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: We didn't have any electricity or anything that all had to be taken care of.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: How did you, did you smoke it?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: The pork we smoked, the sausage we, what you call it, fried it down. Do you know what that means? You fry your little cakes of sausage, you pack them in a stone jar, and you pour the lard that comes out of the sausage over it, And that keeps it sealed tight. And you set it in your cellar where it's cool. And then, as you want it, you just step out of the fridge and cook the pan and warm up, and you have your grease for your gravy or whatever.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And then I canned a lot of meat.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I've never tried that, canning meat. Actually, it scares me.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Oh, really?

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I would worry about not doing it right. For some reason canning applesauce and fruits doesn't (unintelligible). It seems dangerous to can meat.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Oh, I've always canned meat. We like it. It's delicious. And it's handy. there's been times, when the children were home, we'd wonder, what are we gonna have for supper? Well, we put a pound of potatoes on fry, I'd go up to the cellar and I'd bring in a jar of fruit, a jar of tomatoes, a jar of meat.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And there was our our dinner.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Real handy, when you could actually sort of decide that day. Well, now you have to plan two weeks in advance what you're going to eat.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: That's right.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: My my son says, mom, he says, what ever happened to our cellar? he says, I can remember going out there and all those jars of fruit lined up there, and Dad's potatoes in the bin, and apples in the bin, and vegetables sitting there ready to take to the house to fix for dinner and everything like that, he says, I miss that old cellar.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: What is it doing now through summer?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: It's been torn down a long time ago. And, the inside of it has my son's gas diesel tank up in the loft of it, and the oil and things is down in the cellar park. It was above ground cellar.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: So that long time, and our old wood shed's been torn down.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: You just don't use a wood stove anymore.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: No.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you miss it?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: You know, I do. I like the old wood stove. There's lots of times I think, Oh, how nice it'd be to fire up your wood stove again, throw several loaves of bread in the oven and fool around with it. Course, the electric stove's much more convenient. And then that was a chore to get wood.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Yeah, getting wood is a chore. We have a wood stove, and I'm just learning how to cook on it. I mean, it's really an art I found. And I know some things I can do okay. And other things I haven't mastered the art of doing it yet, but I'm, it's the thing that I like the most is the warming ovens.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I, I can't imagine why they ever took those off new stoves, because they just are the handiest things in the world. I would, I would like if they even if they have to have like electric stoves to have little warming ovens because they are just so, so good. And that means that you don't have to finish everything all at the same time, like you do on modern cooking.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Everything has got to finish, right?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yeah. Center. And then put it right on the table.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: And, with our wood stove, you know, if something, you know, I can, I can bake the bread or the rolls or something like that. And when they're done, I put them in the oven and warming up, and I know they're going to stay warm, and then I can be cooking the other stuff. That's right. Okay. And I miss it.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I can't I'm not even that good a cook on my wood stove. And when I'm back, you know, in Moscow not cooking, I mean.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I always liked the old cook stove. I still wish I could cook on again for a little while. I guess that every person, when they get older look back to the old days and think, well, I'd like to do that just once more, I guess. I don't know.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Well, you should have to come up to my cabin. You could cook on my woodstove.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, that would be fun.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: It's, it's fun. It's nice. And I really need a teacher because it's hard to learn these things.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, it's been so long. I'm afraid I'd be a poor teacher right now, but.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I think it's like riding a bicycle. Well, there are so many things that people pass down to each other that they don't even realize, and I've never cooked on a wood stove before. I've got to learn it all by myself from scratch. It's hard.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Which reminds me, how much longer are we going to be here? I have a meatloaf in the oven downstairs, and this turned up kind of (unintelligible).

speaker: Corky Bush
words: We we talked about some of these things, so I'm going to go on. Can you describe some things you and your brothers and sisters did when you were children?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Get into mischief.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Get into mischief. What kinds of things did you do?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, not really too much. My mother and my dad both worked.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Wasn't that pretty unusual?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And I was only nine years old. And I had to take care of my two brothers. Really I can look back and see where I didn't have too much of a childhood. I had to grow up too fast. They were younger than I was, and I had to take care of them. When the folks came home from work at night, I had to have a potatoes peeled and I had to go to store and get the meat, have it ready.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: and then when mom got home, she put it on to cook. And before I went to school in the morning, I had to wash up the breakfast dishes and come home at noon. And. And my grandpa came home at noon, man. And he fixed lunch for the two boys and I. Then of the evening, I had to, like I say, get everything prepared for the evening meal and take watch after my brothers. Well that took place as long as we lived in Clarkston, until we moved up here to the ranch.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And as far as I was concerned, that was about all I. I couldn't go to my girlfriend's houses, play or anything like that. I had to be home. My brothers, they, of course, they played, just like boys.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: They weren't expected to help out as much as you were.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Nothing, only getting in the wood, but they had to make sure the wood was in. And we did have running water and we had electricity after a start. In those days, it was, something to be desired, you know, just a light bulb. And that was about all. We weren't we weren't some of the more fortunate ones.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: We lived quite simply. (unintelligible) I took music class and my mother insisted I take music lessons. And where she found the time to do it, I don't know, but she, did sewing for my music teacher to pay for my music lessons.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I guess it seems a little incongruous that she's expecting you to be home and to work and everything, and then just having you learn music. What do you think she was thinking?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I don't know, I, I just don't know. But she insisted that I take music.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Through that time.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And she bought me a piano. And of course, that helped to pass part of my time while I was looking after my brothers and gave me something to look forward to. My music teacher came to the house.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: My mother did beautiful sewing for her. She made her beautiful clothes.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I was the oldest, and I always resented, you know, not having the freedom I thought that I gave my brothers and sisters.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, I don't know if I resented it at the time, but I think back, and, and I see so many things that I missed.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I just wasn't, I just wasn't a little girl. I had to grow up. I had to have a level head. I remember one day I started a fire in the cook stove, and I didn't, I didn't know the dangers or what was to happen or something, I don't know. Anyway, the fire had gone out and I presume the stove was still warm and I poured cold oil in it, and I got down and opened up the front of the thing and lit it.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, it just popped right out in my face. It burnt my hands terribly bad, burnt all the hair off my face and around the edge. And that was one of the tragedies of being left alone like that.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: What did you do? How did you get help?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I went to one of my neighbors, and they called mom over at the counter, and she came home and took me to the doctor. My hands were burned terribly. Oh, they hurt. I could remember yet how bad they hurt.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Are they scarred badly?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Not too badly.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: The doctor must have done a good job.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: They may not have been burned as bad as I thought they were, but oh, they hurt.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Burns are the worst things. Well, discuss some of the things you remember about your courtship. How did you meet your husband?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, he was just here, and we moved here. Of course I was a new girl at Teakean.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: He had his eye out.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: We just met, I suppose. I don't remember the first time we met. I don't remember where it was. Possibly we passed him on the road somewhere. Going school or something. I just don't remember.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: How did you start courting?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: He made wood for my dad over on our place, and he was there quite awhile. Quite a bit. And I guess that was the start. And then he, it was kind of hard to get around up here in those days, and he'd ask me to go with him to a dance over to Cavendish. And he didn't have a car and he was going to borrow a car.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, he couldn't get the car, so he had to call me up and tell me that we couldn't go to the dance. So then we went down to a sock-hop, to a dance one night, and my folks went along. I didn't trust me I guess. Anyway, we rode the horses down. Mom and dad walked down. So coming home, I.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: We put them on the horses, and sent them on home and we walked. That's the night he proposed.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: How long had you known him before he proposed?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: A couple of years.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: So you actually had sort of dated and courted. Didn't see each other for a long time.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, he didn't go with me very much until just before we were married. He had other girlfriends.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Were you ever jealous of them?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: After we started going together, I was. And when we were first married, terribly jealous, he was too.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: He was too.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: What were some of the reasons that you got married?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Some of the reasons? Love, I guess.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Did you think it should ever have to leave Teakean, or did you pretty much know you could stay?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: You know, I figured that this would be it. And I was a city girl. And now you take a city girl and put her on the farm, and she has to learn everything.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Yeah.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I was raised in the city and then became a farmer's wife.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Was that hard for you early on?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, it all came gradually. His mother, his folks were, they were pioneers of Teakean. They homesteaded here and, they were the some of the early settlers. And she did all these things. And I learned a lot from her.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Was she nice too you? I mean, did she help you learn them or did she?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Not at first, she didn't like me at first.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: She didn't? Did she think you were too citified for her son?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I don't think it would have made much difference who married her son. I don't think she would have been the right one, no matter who it was. But as it turned out, in later years, I was the one that took care of her. I took care of her for about 20 years. Her and her husband

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Did she grow to not?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: She'd grow to think a lot of me and, grandpa has told me a good many times. Lee, I don't know how to do it if it wasn't for you, but at first they they just couldn't accept me at first. That is, she couldn't. Grandpa was pretty good.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: But she just about to think anybody ought to marry her son.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: No. Nobody was good enough for her son. It wouldn't have made any difference who it was.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I think all mothers, to a certain degree are that way.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Yeah. Is that the way, do you think about your daughter in law?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: My daughter in law? I like my daughter in law real well. She's real sweet.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I so you're trying not to act towards her the way you said.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I hope I haven't, evidently I haven't, because I think she thinks the world of us. Because she's real good to us. She's real nice.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: What factors do you think affected the number of children that you had?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: What factors?

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Would you have liked to have more? I guess is really what I'm asking. More or fewer children.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I have, I would have had two more children, but I miscarried. in those days, we didn't have contraceptives and things they have now. And then if you got pregnant, you were pregnant, and that was it.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Were they, were the miscarriages before the (unintelligible)?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: That's the reason there's so much difference between my daughters. They were between that. They were boys.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: So the not having doctors close around and everything was really.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I think so now with, when I, when I was pregnant with Billy, probably I would lost him. But I went to the hospital. I had the, six month, I believe, fifth month. It was right along there where I lost the other two. And, so we saved him by me going to the hospital, and then I was bed fast for the rest of the nine months.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And we finally got our boy. Then we called it quits.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Oh, yes. For four months, you were in the hospital?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I wasn't in the hospital. I had to go home and go to bed. I couldn't be up.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: What did you do? You must, I would have been bored to tears, I think.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, I did what I could for the family in the bed. When they wanted biscuits, they would bring the bread board in and put it on my lap on the bed and bring me what I told them them to bring for the ingredients, and I mix them up, roll them out, cut them, put them in the pan for them, and then they would bake them. The same way with other things. We got by.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: We couldn't afford hired help. We did hire our little niece for a little while to help out. We couldn't afford help constantly, so the family did it. My oldest daughter was old enough to,

speaker: Corky Bush
words: To be of some assistance.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yeah, and to go ahead and help.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: But you hadn't had any trouble with the girls?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: No.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Just just just.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Just the boys. Sounds strange, but that's what it was.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Well, sounds strange, but I certainly believe you. How do you see the future for your grandchildren?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: For my grandchildren?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Some of them I can see where the future looks good. And some of them, I can see where it doesn't look very good.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: What makes the difference?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: What makes the difference? my daughter that is here,

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Who lives in your front yard.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And lives in our front yard. She has some children, that has given her a real hard time. And, I can't see their future being too bright. And my oldest daughter has two children.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: That has given her problems. The one is retarded, and that makes it hard for him. Makes it hard for the family. He's of age now, and I can't see the future being too bright for him. My daughter in Spokane,

speaker: Leah Brown
words: She has pretty good children. Only I can see, I can see where she's,

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Giving them too much rope. They're, they're smoking and they're drinking. And it breaks my heart.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: How old are they?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: They're 14 and 15. Billy's children, I don't think you could ask for, more levelheaded or, or better children in this day and age.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: And how old are they?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Billy is the oldest, and she said she was 12 and junior is seven. Of course now, what will happen later? They're young now. And the little girl that Viola has with her, she's her baby. She's a nice little girl. She's, I think the future looks good for her.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you think any of them will stay in Teakean?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I think Billy's children and Pam will.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: And the rest you see going where?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I don't know, I just don't know. Now, Arlene's two little girls that she has at home are, she says she has no problem with them, but she's had a lot of problem with the other three. But now, the oldest grandson of Arlene just turned out real nice. He lives right down here by Billy, and he has, three little children with him.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: They're building them a house over South Lake and they're. He's turning out pretty good now, but, he got married when he was only 17, I think it was. And, of course, that marriage went on the rocks. But he's married now to this little girl. And they seem to be doing pretty good. So one of Arlene's problems is sort of work itself out.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: But the other two children, I don't know. I guess every family has their their ups and their downs and their problems.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you think that the way children have grown up have change and that that's the difference here?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I think so. It's. And then two divorce. this is the problem with these children is divorce.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: I see.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: That's like the old saying when they're divorced, the children pays. And that's what happened here.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you feel sort of helpless?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yes. Because there's nothing I can do. I, you can advise your children after they're grown and married, but, you can't tell them like you did before, how you got to do this. You've got to do that. You can't do that anymore. And then you can't advise them unless they ask you. Because they feel you're interfering. So that makes a difference, too.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: So you sort of have to sit back and.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: You just have to sit back and watch it and just, just pray that everything's going to be all right.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: That's hard though. I think a hard way to, place to be.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And if I stop and think about it, it would, I would just worry myself sick. And I can't do that because I am sick anyway, and I just can't do it.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Would you mind talking about what you're sick with?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I had open heart surgery.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: You did.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: All right. So that scar, that was, how long ago?

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Four years ago. I was 60.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: A little past 60. I was 65 my last birthday.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Well, you seemed to be doing pretty well.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, yes. I, well, I'm here, and I wouldn't have been here if it hadn't been for open heart surgery.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Where did, where was this done?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: In Spokane, at (unintelligible) hospital. And my husband has cancer.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: So, you know, we are. Do you think that your children come to you enough?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: My children are just wonderful to us. Now, the ones that's away from home, of course, they can't come as often as the others, but they come when they can, and they're there. They're all real good to us. And the daughter that's living, in the trailer house, over by us. She moved down here specially so she could take care of us.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And between her and, my son and his wife, I.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: So you do feel cared for.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: There are lots of parents who aren't feeling that way.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I know, and I think I'm fortunate.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: You talk all the time about being busy. What do you do for recreation and for relaxation?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: For recreation? We sit and watch television. My husband in his recliner chair and me in mine.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: What are your favorite shows?

speaker: Leah Brown

words: Has, has there ever been a time in your life when you had to take the major responsibility for the financial support of your family, like when your husband was sick?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yes. In 1949, my husband got a fever and he was in, Saint Joseph's Hospital down at Lewiston for 21 days. And we didn't know if he was going to live or not.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: We're lucky they knew what he was.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Now, I had to leave the children at home on the ranch. The daughter that's living up by us now was, what was she, 17 or 18? I forget now. And we had cows to milk. We had just bought a hundred little chickens, and she took care of them. And, the other two children, my oldest daughter was married at that time, lived in Lewiston. I stayed with her and I had leave the children on the ranch, and I had to take care of everything.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And again, that's where our good neighbors showed up. They came and put our hay in the barn, and, our son in law at Lewiston did our combine for us. When some of the other neighbors got through with their combining, they came and helped finished ours. (unintelligible) That's right. The the neighbors have always been good that way.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: this community of. Well, we've always felt responsibility toward one another.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: There are people that we've talked to who've lived in communities for 30, 40 and sometimes 50 years who still feel they're not a part of the community. Do you feel that way in Teakean?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I felt that way part of the time that we lived here. I always felt that a lot of the people in the community felt they were a little better than we were, because we were small farmers and we didn't, we couldn't dress our children as nice as some of them could, and we couldn't do some of the things some of them could.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Now, whether they felt that way or not, I don't know. But. I felt that way.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: it seemed like if anybody was ever left out of anything, it was always us,

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yeah. If, Something was done and we helped that seemed like our name somehow or another was always left off. Maybe it wasn't intentional. Could've just happened that way, but it did happen. And so it made us feel that we just weren't part of it. You know, we weren't accepted as part of the community.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Has that ceased?

words: I don't know if they looked down on a person or not. They. I don't have to say that. speaker: Leah Brown
words: And they were hurt that way. they always were clean. They always look nice.

words: (unintelligible)

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yeah. They were, the children, well, the kids, the schools got them. If we don't have them, they don't have anything to do with it. Well, I said, if that's all that they want, their friendship isn't worth it. Just find someone that will accept you as you are and forget about it, because we just can't.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: We can't have Jansen sweaters and and the things that go with them.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: It's hard, though, for children to understand that sometimes.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yeah, but at that age, they. When they went to high school, they they were pretty good. They.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: They finally came around to feeling they were just as good as the next woman. And they just suffered through it.

words: Were there always buses? From (unintelligible).

words: They came over here, the schoolhouse sat right here by the Grange Hall.

words: Because the church and the Grange and the school, at one turn. How did you feel when the school got closed down?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: We felt sad. Of course, they built this other school over at Cavendish, and the children went over there and then they were bussed. Now the only one of our children that was bussed to, over to Cavendish, was Billy. The other children went to this other school.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you miss it, the school and the community?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Well, since I don't have any more children, I don't. But I think it would be nice if there was. Well, the one over at Cavendish works out pretty well.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: How many grades does that go through?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: The eighth. It has all eight grades. And, But of course, at that time we had, there was a school at Cavendish, there was two schools here at Teakean. And they had, oh, they had 20, 30 children go to school at that time, you see, because.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: there still was that many children going to school because, like we said in those days, people were living and making a living on 40 and 60 and 80 acres, you see. So they be a lot of families around. And they could, they could take care of that many children. But for three schools, then there was one, at Cream Ridge too, It was just over the hill here. So.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: That's a lot of schools, actually.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: But they were they had plenty of children going. And then at that time too, this is several years ago, they had a high school at Southwick. speaker: Leah Brown
words: really, I think the children when when they were kept up on the farm and up on the hill away from town, I think they were better children and, than what we have now, when we have to send them to town and it's with the kids, it's taking dope, drinking and, all this stuff. I know my children are just worried about their children having to go where there's so much of that stuff.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And, our little country schools, I think was good for the kids. Of course, that's all done away with. All past now, so we have to.

words: Do you think they'll win?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I think sooner or later they're going to take it. Maybe. Maybe from the sixth grade on up. I don't believe they'll ever take the little children, because I don't really think it's down the street working on the bus. It'd be a long, long trip for the little children.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And, as far as telling them what to do with their children, I, I can't. If they ask me, I do.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Well, if they, just pretend that somebody is asking you, and it's not your own children.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I'd say keep them on the farm as long as you can. Keep right there, as long as you can give them plenty to do. It don't hurt kids to work. That is, if you don't, overload them, you know, but I think it's good for kids to work and let them learn. I like my son.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: He wanted the car. Well, I says I'm not going to buy your car. If you get a car, you got to make your own money. You got to get it yourself. And ever since he was 12 years old, he's got a bank account. When his dad would go out to thrash, he'd go out into the field with him.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And there's always some around the edge that the combine or the, at that time, they had a binder, that it doesn't always get. So he took him a spoon and a little sieve and a little backup. speaker: Leah Brown
words: It was all nice and clean. Think so. And then when he wanted the car, I said, you just got to find a way to make the money to buy your car.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And I said, dad, I'll furnish the gas because we don't want any of this going to the neighbors and swiping gas. And, but we said we'd furnish the gas. But you got to get your own car. You got pay for your own license and your own insurance. And he found a way to do it, and he got him a car.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: (unintelligible)

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And he knew how to take care of it, because he knew if that was gone, he'd have to make money to get him another one, which, he did go through 2 or 3 before he finally settled down.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Did any of them ever have any accidents?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: He never had an accident. No. He's always been a good driver. Sometimes I think he drives too fast. I think all young fellows do. But so far he hasn't had an accident.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you worry about the future for yourself?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: For myself? I don't worry about it. I wonder sometimes what would happen if, if we had to, to be sick or in a rest home for any length of time, and I tell my children that, I don't want them to be burdened with me, that if they are, it's their own fault that I don't want to be a burden to my children.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And, as long as I can get around, take care of myself, I hope I can live. But when I can't, I don't want to live.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you have Social Security, and?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: We have Social Security. We have, Medicare, and we have, medical service. But we don't have any life insurance. Either one of us. So. But we sold our 160 acres to our son, and, we do have enough stashed away to bury us in case of death from that. Other than that, he pays us so much each year on the place.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And then with our Social Security, that's how we live.

words: And do you still can and stuff like that?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Oh, yes.

words: So you do a lot of living off the the land, too.

words: I can't do any gardening or anything like that. Our daughter and.

words: Sister.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Gardening and, but she helps me can. We put pretty, almost 100 years of corn in the deep freeze the other day. We can a lot of stuff, but we have our, we still have our own meat. And, so we do all right.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I like, I like the Ladies Home Journal, and I like, Good Housekeeping, and, I like the Rural Light. speaker: Leah Brown
words: And that's about it. I think that's it.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And my Bible. I read my Bible a lot. I, I.

words: Do you go to church? I've been meaning to ask you. Where do you go to church? Do you get, do you get over to Cavendish?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Now, I go, when I go to church, I go over to Cream Ridge.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: There's still a church there.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: But it's been, almost a year since I've been there. It seems like something is just kept me from going. I don't know what. I just don't know. I just, for the last year, I just haven't, something just has.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Pressured me to stay away. I don't know why. Because it's a good church, and I don't know why. I just haven't wanted to go.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you feel it's the distance? Or is it the fact that it's not really your community or?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yep, it isn't our community. And I don't belong to the church. Yeah, but I. I just go to go to church and Sunday school. It is a good church. The people make me feel welcome. There is no, friction there at all, they make you feel real welcome. But it seems like either in Sunday morning I either have company or it's snowing.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: In the summertime we have lots the company, almost every Sunday. Then in the wintertime the roads get bad and I feel, well, maybe I shouldn't go. And then part of the year this year we were both sick, we both had pneumonia and it took us a long time to get over that. And it seems like it's just been something like that to keep us from going.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you feel though you're able to sustain your faith here by yourself?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I think so. We both watch church Sunday mornings on the TV. We play and sing church songs a lot. I read my Bible a lot. My husband isn't too religious, he believes, but that's about it.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Why do you think that is? That seems really to be true. A lot women we talk to will say that my husband's not as religious as I am or something like that.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: So I don't know why that is. But you know what it comes down to? To faith and believing. Things are going to be all right. He has a stronger faith in things like that than I do. I get worried and crap and stew. It isn't going to work out. It isn't going to work out. And according to the Bible, that is being a good Christian, you know you're supposed to have faith enough to know it's going to.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: But, I'm the one that always worries about it. And he says it's going to be all right.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Maybe it's just different kinds of faith and different kinds of beliefs and.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: That could be, I don't know.

words: What are the most common things that Gifford asks you about? Well, looking back over the whole, over the years.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: That he asks me about?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I don't know.

words: What things? What things in particular do you.

words: Well, people give all kinds of answers. Is does he ever ask you about the family or how the children are going or does he ask you about.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Does he ask you about what's going on in the world? Has he asked you about politics? I, there are just all kinds of things.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: He doesn't usually ask me. He usually tells me, oh, he's that type. I've always more or less leaned on him for advice and things like that, and I think I made a mistake. I think I should have been more,

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Less leaning?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yeah, yeah. took more of a stand against things. I always would just give in and say, okay, we'll do it your way.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Even when you really didn't want to.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yeah. And I think I should have stood up for my rights. And really. Said we're going to do it this way, but I didn't. I'd say we'll do it your way. And so naturally. speaker: Corky Bush
words: Is this more now? More recently?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Yes. As he gets older and more dependent on me, it comes more that way now.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: And you would have liked that relationship even earlier in your marriage.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I think I would have come to think of it now, as I look back, I think I would have. Because, he made decisions that if I were doing it, and since I look back now, I think we would have been a little better off. I think I'm a better manager than he was.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: And of course he never, since he never said what it is you wanted, you never really got a chance to make a choice.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: No, no, I never made any decisions. I let him make them. And I think I should have, because, like I say, I think I can manage better than what he did.

words: Is there anything else you want to tell me?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Oh, I don't know. What would you like to know?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: Anything I want to tell you.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: You would be. You'd be a good secretary.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: And, my music, I believe I would've went on with my music. Music was hard for me. I, I didn't have any musical talent at all. It just had to be drummed into my head. speaker: Leah Brown
words: I, both playing the piano and singing. Pearl's daughter and I, we have played and sang for, oh, I don't know how many funerals and weddings and things. speaker: Leah Brown
words: But of course, now they go to the, funeral parlors anymore now, and they have the organ things. Of course, I could play the organ with a little practice. I go down to my brother's, and she has an organ, and I, I would love to have an organ, but,

speaker: Leah Brown
words: I believe I would have, like. I believe I'd have been happier if I went on to school. A little further anyway.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Just maybe to high school.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: At least through high school.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: And learn some of these things.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: That's right.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: No.

words: Do you think he wishes he would?

words: He tells his grandchildren, you get you an education. I think he would, because he's always, and he insisted that our children go through high school, and, they're all glad that he did. speaker: Corky Bush
words: So you weren't really antagonistic towards education?

speaker: Leah Brown
words: No.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Do you wish that, that maybe you'd gotten away from Teakean and gone to another, to a city, or traveled more, or done more things?

words: If we'd have got away from Teakean?

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Well, no, just that might be one option. Did you do you wish you'd traveled more? Been more places?

words: I love to travel. Yes, I love to travel. My husband doesn't, but I love to go. As long as my parents lived, I went down to see them at least once a year, sometimes twice a year. speaker: Leah Brown
words: We've just, we go to Lewiston, maybe Spokane, that's it. And that was our dream. After we got our children raised, we were going to travel, go and see things, but neither one of us were in a condition to to do it now. So I say, when you're young, do things.

speaker: Corky Bush
words: Because you may not when you're older.

speaker: Leah Brown
words: When you get older, you may not. My husband gets a little irritated at me for telling our children they'll take off and go, you know, and just walk off and leave things, well they know Mom and Dad look after them see, and he gets a little irritated at me because I encourage them to go. speaker: Leah Brown
words: You might not get to them when you get older.
